revision.title: Exploit Exposure Layer: Free Data on Every Wallet Still Approved to an Exploited Contract
revision.summary: After an exploit, the token approvals users granted to the exploited contract stay live and keep getting drained, sometimes for years. Revoke.cash will scan every supported chain for every contract on its public exploit list, compute which wallets are still exposed, and serve that data through a free API so any wallet or explorer can warn its own users. The multichain exploit check on Revoke.cash moves out of the paid tier and becomes free, and a public metrics page tracks exposure, revocations, and value at risk per exploit.

sections.why:
Exploited contracts do not stop draining when the news cycle ends. Radiant Capital's lending pools on Arbitrum and BNB Chain were taken over in October 2024, and the attacker's implementation is still installed. It still calls transferFrom on wallets with open approvals: about 2,200 wallets were drained in 2025 and about 170 more in 2026 through September 13, all to one receiver address (0x070ca92f568037d351666b3918a0f6ba7ad20ed1), with the latest drain two days before this was written. Radiant's DAO scoped these approval losses at $7.7M for 2024 and $1.2M for the first quarter of 2025 and did not compensate them. Revoking is the only protection those wallets have.

The same pattern repeats at every scale. Multichain disclosed a router bug on January 18, 2022 and asked users to revoke; the first drain came 16 hours later, and a month on 3,101 of 7,962 affected addresses still had not revoked (Multichain post-mortem). During that incident Multichain built an ad-hoc approval-revoke API that SushiSwap, SpookySwap and AAVE integrated to warn users. Multichain is gone and nothing replaced it. In January 2026 SwapNet drained $13.43M from 18 Matcha users, 17 of them in the 45 minutes between the first attack and the pause (Matcha post-mortem).

Today a user learns they are exposed only by opening the Revoke.cash page for that exploit, one chain at a time. Wallets and explorers have no data source to warn their own users. After this initiative, any wallet can tell a user "you are still approved to exploit X on chain Y" the moment they open it, and anyone can check the ecosystem-wide numbers.
sections.in_scope:
- **Chain-wide exposure scan per exploit.** For every contract on the exploit list, all approval events across the whole chain are read, the set of wallets with a live allowance is computed, and it is kept current as users approve and revoke. Covers ERC-20, ERC-721 and Permit2 allowances on every supported network.
- **Public exposure API, free and unauthenticated.** Per exploit: exposed wallets per chain and the affected spenders. Per address: exposed to any listed exploit, all chains in one call. Rate limited, open data license, with integration documentation so any wallet or explorer can warn its own users.
- **Free multichain exploit check on Revoke.cash.** Any user checks any address against all listed exploits on every chain at once, backed by the same API. Today this is a Premium feature.
- **Public metrics page with an automated impact pipeline.** For every listed exploit, per chain and in total: wallets exposed, wallets that revoked within 72 hours of listing, time from exploit to listing, value exposed at exploit time, value protected by revocations made before the exploit, and value still at risk today. Prevention is counted ecosystem-wide, from any tool. The pipeline runs on listing and on a schedule, prices assets with a maintained source, and publishes its methodology. Results are also served through the API.
sections.out_scope:
- Push alerts of any kind from Revoke.cash for free users. Wallets deliver warnings inside their own UI. Revoke.cash's paid tiers keep push monitoring and automated revoking on top of the free layer.
- Automated revoking.
- Tracing stolen funds to attacker addresses. The metrics show exposed value, not confirmed theft.
- Attributing prevented value to Revoke.cash or any single tool.
- Changes to how exploits get listed. The public exploit list on GitHub and its submission template stay as they are.
- A general spender risk dataset.
sections.team:
**Rosco Kalis** does the work. He created Revoke.cash in 2019 as the first token approval management tool and has worked on it full-time since 2022, growing it to 100+ networks, NFT and Permit2 support, batch revoking, and the exploit checker. He maintains the public exploit list and the spender data this initiative builds on. Revoke.cash received Optimism RetroPGF funding and is the tool protocols point their users to after an incident, most recently in Matcha's SwapNet post-mortem.

Track record: https://github.com/rkalis, https://x.com/RoscoKalis, https://revoke.cash/about.

No other funder pays for this scope. The Optimism Foundation and the Monad Foundation sponsor batch revoke fees on their chains, which is unrelated to this work.
sections.why_grant:
- The public exploit list: 67 documented approval exploits with contract addresses per chain, a submission template, and per-exploit pages with a single-chain checker at https://revoke.cash/exploits
- Chain coverage: Revoke.cash already indexes approvals on 100+ EVM networks, with the RPC, log-provider and block-range handling that a chain-wide scan needs
- An exploit fan-out already running in the Revoke.cash indexer for its automated revoking, which re-evaluates known wallets when an exploit is listed (open source in the repository, packages/core/lib/auto-revoke)
- The impact methodology: scripts that compute value exposed at exploit time, value protected by earlier revocations, and value still at risk, with a token price mapping built up over two years (apps/web/scripts/exploits)
- Spender risk data with exploit labels, and existing embeds in Ledger, Safe, World App and Farcaster that give direct lines to wallet teams

A from-scratch team would pay for chain coverage, the exploit list and the pricing work before writing the first line of exposure code. That is why this is $100,000 and not a from-scratch price.
sections.commitments:
- The exposure engine, API and pipeline are published under MIT; the exposure and metrics data under CC BY 4.0.
- We maintain the scan, the API and the metrics page for at least 12 months after the last milestone at no further cost.
- Pinned target: at least 3 third-party integrations in production within 9 months of the first payment.
- The free layer covers pull: any address, any chain, any listed exploit, with no subscription. No exception requested.

milestones.name: Exposure engine, public API and free multichain check
criteria: Chain-wide exposure sets computed for every contract on the exploit list on every supported network, covering ERC-20, ERC-721 and Permit2 allowances, refreshed as approvals and revocations land, and shown live on each exploit page

Public API live with documentation and no authentication, returning per-exploit exposed wallet counts per chain and a per-address check across all listed exploits and all chains in one call, with the code published under MIT
The multichain exploit check on revoke.cash available without a subscription, backed by the API
Integration documentation for wallets and explorers published

milestones.name: Public metrics page and automated impact pipeline
criteria: Metrics page live for every listed exploit, per chain and in total: wallets exposed, wallets that revoked within 72 hours of listing, time from exploit to listing, value exposed at exploit time, value protected by revocations before the exploit, and value still at risk
Pipeline runs automatically on every new listing and on a schedule, covering ERC-20, ERC-721 and Permit2
Methodology published, including the pricing source and the ecosystem-wide counting rule

milestones.name: Adoption
criteria: At least 3 third-party wallets or explorers show exposure warnings in production through the public API, each confirmed by a public announcement or page from that party; Revoke.cash's own embeds do not count

At least 1,500 distinct wallets revoked an allowance to a contract on the exploit list during a 90-day window after the API launch, counted from on-chain ERC-20 revocation events on the same basis as the published baseline of 1,238 wallets for June 17 to September 15, 2026 (exploits not marked fixed
The metrics page has been public for at least 3 months with its methodology published
